column3: Immediate context supplies the same reduction of the messenger to a man, now joined to the charge of possession.
Directly identifies inventing a lie about Allah as unauthorized human speech presented as divine judgment.
Pairs fabrication about Allah with denying His signs, but largely repeats the focus accusation in general form.
A people explicitly refuse belief in their messenger after rejecting his evidence and retaining inherited gods.
The next generation continues the local messenger cycle but adds no detail to the accusation at 23:38.
Again joins inventing lies about Allah with rejecting truth, though the core relation is already established.
Shows a settled refusal to believe that reclassifies every sign as magic.
The immediately preceding prophet appeals for help specifically because his people called him a liar.
Betrayal of Allah and the messenger does not clarify the public charge that revelation is fabricated.
Repeats the fabrication-and-denial pattern with little new beyond earlier examples.
Answers the claim of fabrication with a bounded challenge to produce a comparable surah.
The opening success of believers provides a local contrary horizon to the refusal to believe in the messenger.
Explicitly denies that the message is poetry and defines it as clear remembrance and Quran.
The local successor narrative again sends a human messenger with a call to worship Allah alone.
Records the combined claims that the messenger is merely a man, his message fabricated, and the truth magic.
Condemns lying about Allah, but repeats the central fabrication theme without a new messenger dynamic.
The local account calls the preceding events signs and a test, only indirectly bearing on the accusation.
The warning against deniers provides a broad consequence but no added account of fabricated revelation.
Refusal to believe is tied to protecting inherited practice and imputing worldly ambition to the messengers.
Directly reverses the focus accusation: those who do not believe Allah's signs are the fabricators and liars.
Combines the exact alternatives of lying about Allah or possession with refusal to believe in the Hereafter.
Returning to false worship is described as inventing a lie about Allah, extending fabrication to religious allegiance.
The earlier Noah scene establishes the same local pattern of a human messenger calling his people to exclusive worship.
The repeated woe for deniers adds little after the earlier occurrence.
Moses warns against fabricating lies about Allah and states the destructive outcome of doing so.
Local believers are characterized by faith in their Lord's signs, the direct opposite of the focus response.
Intensive denial of divine signs sharpens the focus group's refusal to credit the messenger.
False professions of faith contrast with explicit disbelief, but do not address the fabrication charge.
Raises the Day of Judgment consequence for those who fabricate lies about Allah.
Calling a messenger a sorcerer and liar is a relevant accusation, but adds little detail.
Tests the messenger's claim conditionally and distinguishes his personal lie from the risk that his warning is true.
Immediate local precedent presents the elite dismissing Noah as a man like themselves and appealing to ancestral custom.
Another refrain condemning deniers, now redundant within the list.
False legal classifications are named as lies about Allah made without knowledge and used to mislead others.
Their verbal acknowledgement of Allah exposes a local inconsistency but does not itself explain the accusation.
The question of what discourse people will believe after this is a direct challenge to continued disbelief.
General majority disbelief adds little to the specific claim that a messenger fabricated revelation.
Defines the Quranic account as not invented speech but confirmation, guidance, and mercy for believers.
A parallel fabrication challenge is already supplied more directly by 10:38.
Divine sending and preservation of the remembrance directly counters its portrayal as a human fabrication.
Immediate local continuation again reduces the messenger to a human like the audience while denying the Hereafter.
Explicitly denies that the message is a poet's speech and rebukes the scarcity of belief.
The account of illicit teaching and magic is too indirect to explain this claim about a messenger's revelation.
The repeated woe for deniers is now largely redundant.
The final occurrence of the same refrain adds no distinct clarification.
Challenges the recipient of the Quran by social status, extending objections to the messenger's human suitability.
Immediate speech treats obedience to a human messenger as loss, making the local resistance explicit.
Denial and turning away are relevant only as a general pattern of rejection.
False speech about Allah's having a child supplies another concrete form of ungrounded divine attribution.
The later elite arrogance continues the local resistance pattern without adding to the speech accusation.
Provision and security do not clarify the claim that the messenger fabricated a lie.
Questions surprise that a reminder came through a man from among the people, directly addressing human-messenger resistance.
Immediate local skepticism about resurrection supplies the content behind the wider refusal to accept the messenger.
Denial of the Day of Judgment is a broader companion to disbelief, without the fabrication charge.
The assertion of Allah's sole divinity does not add to this accusation-and-refusal exchange.
The local sequence generalizes the pattern: each community denied its messenger and became a reusable story.
The generic woe for deniers is already well covered by earlier refrains.
Exact human-like-us dismissal is joined to a direct judgment that the messenger is among the liars.
Immediate ridicule of the promised future clarifies the local content of their unbelief.
Places the messenger's denial within a recurring history of rejecting clear proofs and illuminating scripture.
The people call their messenger human like themselves and demand a sign to validate his truthfulness.
Local contrast between truth and their desires explains why the received reminder is turned away.
A procedural question about theft and punishment does not illuminate fabricated revelation or belief.
Refusing belief in Allah and His messenger supplies a direct contrary frame, though without the accusation's wording.
A man urges his people to follow the messengers, offering a positive response to the kind of call rejected at the focus.
Immediate later verdict states that truth came to them and they are the liars, reversing their charge against the messenger.
Condemns fabrication about Allah after evidence, but is redundant with stronger formulations above.
Immediate preceding verse explicitly denies resurrection and concludes that they will not be raised or believe.
The heart not lying about what it saw offers only a distant contrast to their accusation of lying.
Reports the accusation that the Quran was fabricated with human assistance and identifies it as falsehood.
Immediate consequence announces that the deniers will soon become regretful.
A false claim about Allah is directly labeled a lie, though it concerns divine offspring rather than revelation.
The Quran's differing effects on believers and wrongdoers only indirectly address the focus response.
Hostility toward messengers follows an unfounded omen accusation, but not a fabrication claim.
Making one's provision into denial is a limited parallel for responding to divine gift with rejection.
The people combine the human-like-us objection with denial of revelation and an accusation of lying.
Immediate continuation has the prophet seek divine help because of their denial.
A human warner is met with astonishment and labeled a magician and habitual liar.
Belief in divine signs is linked to receptive hearing and submission, clarifying the positive alternative to refusal.
Noah's rescue and praise are part of the local narrative but do not add to the accusation at issue.
False religious claims are condemned as lying and ungrateful, but the intermediary-worship setting is indirect.
Directly voices the charge of fabricating a lie about Allah and answers it with divine effacement of falsehood.
The creation of later generations only continues the local chronology.
Lists earlier peoples who denied, providing only a broad historical parallel.
The denial of punishment does not clarify the human-fabrication charge.
Resurrection is part of the surah's larger argument but is distant from this immediate accusation.
A crisis-driven claim of belief distinguishes pressured assent from the sustained trust denied at the focus.
Belief or doubt about the Hereafter is relevant only indirectly to belief in the messenger.
The fullest counterfeit-revelation parallel: claiming unwarranted revelation and an equivalent divine descent is lying about Allah.
Forbidding compliance with deniers marks their rejection as a pressure to be resisted.
Divine mercy and knowledge do not clarify the accusation or the refusal to believe.
A messenger's self-description as trustworthy directly counters the claim that he fabricated speech about Allah.
Family nursing obligations do not bear on the messenger's truthfulness or the audience's disbelief.
Calling the events a sign for believers supplies a general contrast to those who will not believe.
The mistaken human-versus-angel classification is only a distant parallel to objections based on human status.
Moses' clear signs are dismissed as fabricated magic and rejected through appeal to ancestral precedent.
Competing loyalties and divine command do not add to this fabrication accusation.
Belief delayed until painful punishment clarifies the severity of the refusal expressed at the focus.
Marriage conduct and not mocking Allah's signs do not clarify the messenger's alleged fabrication.
Faith and righteous works offer a very broad contrary profile, with no new detail about revelation's source.
Explicitly condemns inventing a lie about Allah, naming the central offense of the focus.
Directly rejects the claim that Allah has revealed nothing to any human, answering the human-messenger objection.
Pairs inventing a lie about Allah with denying His signs in a closely parallel indictment.
Challenges people who make lawful and unlawful classifications, asking whether Allah authorized them or they invented lies about Him.
Noah's people say he is only a human like them and explicitly refuse to believe him, closely matching the focus response.
Directly takes up the accusation that the Quranic message was fabricated and distinguishes the speaker's liability if it were so.
The messengers answer their people's doubt by grounding their call in Allah, clarifying the setting of contested prophetic authority.
Messengers concede shared humanity while affirming that Allah favors whom He wills, directly answering the objection to a human messenger.
Those addressed by the revealed Reminder call its recipient mad, a direct alternate dismissal of revelation.
People attribute what they dislike to Allah while their tongues assert lies, supplying another form of false divine attribution.
Directly reports the claim that a human teaches the Prophet and rejects that account of the revelation's source.
The wrongdoers say the audience follows a bewitched man, closely paralleling the reduction of the messenger to a defective human.
Identifies the objection that Allah sent a human messenger as what prevented people from believing.
Condemns those who assert divine partners without proof as inventing a lie about Allah.
The deniers call the messenger merely human and the received message obvious magic, combining both focus-side objections.
They cycle through dreams, fabrication, poetry, and a demand for a sign, directly cataloguing rival explanations for revelation.
The same surah asks whether they say there is madness in him, completing the local repertoire of dismissal.
Objects to the messenger's ordinary eating and movement in markets, extending the human-status objection.
The opponents call him a bewitched man and warn others not to follow him, matching the focus's refusal of trust.
Mockery that this is the one Allah sent as messenger exposes contempt for the chosen human bearer.
Pharaoh's circle calls Moses mad, a further accusation used to discredit a human messenger.
Salih's people class him among those bewitched, showing another non-evidential dismissal of a prophetic claim.
The refusal to abandon inherited gods for a mad poet joins tradition-protection to degrading the messenger's speech.
Directly joins lying about Allah with denying the truth when it comes, a concise parallel to the focus's twofold refusal.
The messenger's shared humanity is explicitly paired with revelation to him, supplying the positive answer to the focus objection.
When truth comes, the people call it magic and declare their disbelief, closely matching the response pattern.
Directly asks about the claim that he fabricated the message and denies that opponents could protect him from Allah if it were true.
The Prophet is explicitly cleared of being a soothsayer or madman, answering familiar discrediting labels.
States the exact charge that he fabricated it, then identifies their unbelief as the operative issue.
Noah's people deny Allah's servant and call him mad, a close narrative antecedent to the focus's local pattern.
Rejects following a single human from among them and calls the resulting claim error and madness.
Condemns one who invents a lie about Allah while being invited to submission, linking fabrication to refusal of the divine call.
Identifies false speech against Allah as an outrageous claim circulated by the foolish.
Calls the revelation inherited magic, a direct humanly mediated reclassification of its source.
Names the accusation that the revelation is nothing but human speech, directly opposing the focus ayah's divine-source claim.
Clears the companion of madness, addressing a recurrent charge against the messenger.
Denies that the Quran is the speech of an accursed satan, rejecting another false explanation of its source.
Condemns those who write a text with their hands and claim it is from Allah, a concrete model of false sacred attribution.
Exposes people who twist scripture with their tongues and claim it is from Allah when it is not.
States that this Quran could not have been fabricated apart from Allah and identifies it as confirmation and detailed exposition.
Warns of pressure to induce the Prophet to fabricate something other than what was revealed, marking fabrication as the contrary to authorized transmission.
Directly answers the charge that it was fabricated by affirming it as truth from the Lord and a warning to an unwarned people.
Challenges the fabrication claim by demanding comparable discourse if the deniers are truthful.
Positively identifies the message as a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.
States that, had the messenger fabricated sayings about Allah, he would have been seized, sharply distinguishing revelation from invention.
